qs.q: A 28-year-old woman with a history of pelvic inflammatory disease (PID) presents with severe abdominal pain and vaginal spotting. Her pregnancy test is positive. What is the most common long-term complication of salpingitis that could explain her current presentation?
o: Ectopic pregnancy due to tubal damage
qs.e: Salpingitis, a component of PID, causes inflammation and scarring of the fallopian tubes, significantly increasing the risk of ectopic pregnancy. While infertility and chronic pelvic pain are also common sequelae, ectopic pregnancy is a critical and frequent complication directly related to tubal damage.
qs.s: Outline of Female Reproductive Pathology: MCQs

qs.q: A young woman with gonococcal pelvic inflammatory disease is counseled about potential long-term complications. What is a well-recognized common sequela of this infection?
qs.e: Pelvic inflammatory disease (PID) from Neisseria gonorrhoeae causes tubal scarring and adhesions, leading to infertility in 10-20% of patients after a single episode. Urethral strictures and cervical cancer are associated with different etiologies.

qs.q: A 38-year-old woman with a history of chronic pelvic inflammatory disease undergoes an endometrial biopsy. Histology reveals a neutrophilic infiltrate in the superficial endometrium and glands, along with a prominent stromal lymphoplasmacytic infiltrate and lymphoid follicles. What is the most likely pathogen associated with the prominent lymphoid follicles in this condition?
qs.e: Chronic endometritis characterized by prominent lymphoid follicles is more commonly associated with Chlamydia infection. Neisseria gonorrhoeae typically causes acute purulent inflammation rather than prominent lymphoid follicles.
qs.s: Female Reproductive Pathology: HPV, Cancer, PCOS & Pregnancy: MCQs

qs.q: An organism is isolated from a patient with pelvic inflammatory disease and postpartum fever, and it is recognized as a cell wall-deficient bacterium. Which species is it?
qs.e: Mycoplasma hominis causes pelvic inflammatory disease and postpartum fever. Mycoplasma pneumoniae primarily causes atypical pneumonia and tracheobronchitis.

qs.q: A woman develops gonococcal pelvic inflammatory disease (PID). What is the most common sequela?
o: Inability to conceive due to infertility
qs.e: Gonococcal PID can lead to a range of serious long-term complications, including ectopic pregnancy, chronic pelvic pain, and infertility, due to scarring and inflammation of the reproductive organs.

qs.q: A 20 year old woman who reports unprotected sex with a new partner 2 weeks previously develop fever and left lower quadrant abdominal pain with onset in association with her menstrual period. The diagnosis is gonococcal pelvic inflammatory disease. What is the common sequela of this infection?
qs.e: Pelvic inflammatory disease (PID) from N. gonorrhoeae causes tubal scarring and adhesions, leading to infertility (10-20% after one episode, higher with recurrent infections) and increased ectopic pregnancy risk. Chronic pelvic pain is also common.

qs.q: A 24-year-old woman presents with primary infertility. Laparoscopy shows fibrous adhesions and dilated fallopian tubes filled with fluid. Which condition is most likely? Usually from prior pelvic inflammatory disease scarring the tube shut, causing fluid accumulation. ---
o: Hydrosalpinx, a fluid‑filled dilated fallopian tube
Cervical stenosis, narrowing of the cervical canal
Twin ectopic pregnancy, simultaneous implantation of two embryos outside the uterus
Uterine fibroids, benign smooth‑muscle tumors of the uterus
Ovarian cyst, a fluid‑filled sac arising from the ovary
qs.e: Hydrosalpinx results from tubal scarring causing fluid accumulation and infertility.

qs.q: A common long-term complication of gonococcal pelvic inflammatory disease (PID) is:
qs.e: Pelvic inflammatory disease (PID), often caused by Neisseria gonorrhoeae or Chlamydia trachomatis, can lead to scarring and inflammation of the reproductive organs, resulting in chronic pelvic pain and infertility.

ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: Pelvic inflammatory disease (PID) is an ascending infection of the upper genital tract, most often from sexually transmitted organisms. Early recognition and broad‑spectrum antibiotics prevent infertility and ectopic pregnancy.

sections.p: PID is inflammation of the uterus, tubes, or ovaries caused by bacterial invasion. Diagnosis relies on clinical criteria plus laboratory support.
b: History of sexual activity, pain, fever, abnormal discharge

t.b: Detect cervical motion tenderness, adnexal tenderness; positive findings support PID

t.a: NAAT for Chlamydia trachomatis and Neisseria gonorrhoeae
t.b: Identifies common pathogens; a positive result confirms etiology and guides therapy
Leukocytosis suggests infection; normal counts do not exclude PID
Elevated values support inflammation but are nonspecific

sections.p: Severity is graded by the CDC 2015 criteria: mild, moderate, severe, or fulminant. Fulminant PID requires hospitalization and IV antibiotics.
b: Mild: low fever, mild pain; moderate: higher fever, moderate pain; severe: high fever, significant pain; fulminant: septic shock, organ failure

sections.p: The leading causes are sexually transmitted infections, especially chlamydia and gonorrhea. Other bacteria and local factors also contribute.

t.b: HIV infection increases PID risk and severity
May alter flora and mask symptoms

sections.p: Patients report lower abdominal pain, fever, and abnormal vaginal discharge. Cervical motion tenderness is a key sign.

t.b: Central pelvic pain suggests tubo‑ovarian involvement; flank pain may indicate pyosalpinx

sections.p: Laboratory and imaging confirm diagnosis and rule out mimics.

t.b: Detects tubo‑ovarian abscess, free fluid, or ovarian cysts; normal in early PID
Rule out ectopic pregnancy if pregnancy test positive

sections.p: Complications can be life‑threatening and include sepsis, abscess, infertility, and ectopic pregnancy.
Treat empirically with broad‑spectrum antibiotics covering gonorrhea, chlamydia, and anaerobes. Adjust therapy based on culture and local resistance.
b: IV therapy for severe cases: ceftriaxone + metronidazole + azithromycin
Monitor for treatment failure or complications

sections.p: Ensure treatment completion, test‑treat‑treat (partner notification), and counsel on barrier contraception.

t.b: Rule out pregnancy before prescribing certain antibiotics

sections.p: Differential diagnoses include ectopic pregnancy, ovarian torsion, appendicitis, and urinary tract infection.
Normal CBC or ultrasound does not exclude PID; low-grade fever may be missed.
b: Normal leukocyte count in early PID
Pregnancy test false negative if early pregnancy

whenToSeekHelp: Evidence of ectopic pregnancy (positive pregnancy test with abdominal pain)

faq.q: Can PID happen without sexual activity?
faq.a: Rarely; non‑sexual routes include post‑operative infection or contaminated tampons, but sexual transmission is the main route.
Yes, with appropriate antibiotics; however, scarring can lead to infertility or ectopic pregnancy.

faq.q: Do I need to see a doctor if I have mild pain?
faq.a: Any pelvic pain with abnormal discharge or fever warrants evaluation to rule out PID.
